preamble: Retroflexion of the alveolar or dental stop [t] to [ʈ]. In Indo-Aryan it is a progressive assimilation: after the retroflex sibilant [ʂ] (itself from the RUKI change and from Indo-Iranian *š), a following *t became ṭ, so Proto-Indo-Iranian *Haštā́ 'eight' gives Sanskrit aṣṭā́ against Avestan ašta. The same mapping recurs in contact: speakers of Indian languages, which contrast dental and retroflex stops, perceive English alveolar /t/ as retroflex, so Indian English uses [ʈ] for /t/ and Hindi borrows English t as ṭ (ṭikaṭ 'ticket'). Cluster coalescence such as Scandinavian rt > ʈ and Tibetan tr- > ʈʂ is a different process and is not included.

examples.note: The *t retroflexed after the preceding retroflex sibilant; Avestan ašta keeps t.
Past participle of dṛś 'see' with the suffix -ta.
Speakers of Indian languages perceive English alveolar /t/ as closer to their retroflex stops than to their dentals.

examples.to: [ʃʈap] (parts of Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar)
examples.note: The retroflex /t/ also turns the preceding /s/ into [ʃ].
Hindi writes all English alveolar stops with its retroflex letters.
